summary: Marker PDU Aligned Framing is an adaptation layer between TCP and DDP that keeps higher-level record boundaries while preserving reliable, in-order delivery. It works with existing TCP implementations. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: TCP carries bytes in order but does not mark the boundaries between higher-level records. MPA adds framing so DDP can identify each record and, with suitable support, place data before all TCP segments arrive in order.

questions: what is marker pdu aligned framing
subtitle: How MPA preserves DDP record boundaries while carrying data over TCP.

tldr.problem: TCP delivers an ordered byte stream without record boundaries, while Direct Data Placement needs to locate each record, including when segments arrive out of order.
tldr.mechanism: MPA wraps each DDP record in an FPDU with a length, padding, and CRC32c. Optional markers at fixed intervals help a receiver locate frame starts in an out-of-order stream.
tldr.outcome: MPA preserves TCP's reliable, in-order delivery while exposing record boundaries to DDP. RFC 5044 is updated by RFC 6581 and RFC 7146.

today: RFC 5044 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2007. It has been updated by RFC 6581 and RFC 7146.

sections.title: Why MPA Adds Framing to TCP
sections.content:
Marker PDU Aligned Framing (MPA) sits between the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and the Direct Data Placement protocol (DDP). DDP needs to identify the boundaries of its records, called Upper Layer Protocol Data Units (ULPDUs). TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery but presents data as a byte stream without those record boundaries.

MPA uses control information at known positions in the stream rather than looking for a special value that could also occur in user data. This deterministic framing lets a receiver locate ULPDUs, including when TCP segments arrive out of order. MPA can use existing TCP implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP provides a byte stream but does not say where DDP records begin and end. MPA adds framing so a receiver can find those record boundaries.

sections.title: The Framed Protocol Data Unit
sections.content:
MPA places exactly one ULPDU in each Framed Protocol Data Unit (FPDU). An FPDU begins with a 16-bit ULPDU_Length, followed by the ULPDU, zero to three padding octets, and a 32-bit cyclic redundancy check (CRC) field. Padding makes the FPDU length a multiple of four.

The length counts only the ULPDU, not the FPDU header, padding, CRC, or markers. The CRC field is always present. When CRCs are enabled, it contains a CRC32c over the FPDU; when disabled by agreement, the field is not checked.
sections.plainLanguage: Each record has its own frame with a length field, optional padding, and a CRC check value. The receiver removes these framing fields before passing the record to DDP.

sections.title: Markers Locate Frames in the Stream
sections.content:
A Marker is four octets: a 16-bit reserved field and a 16-bit FPDUPTR. When markers are enabled, the sender inserts them every 512 octets in TCP sequence space, starting immediately before the first FPDU in full operation.

The FPDUPTR points backward from the marker to the beginning of the FPDU's ULPDU_Length field. If a marker falls between FPDUs, its pointer is zero and the next FPDU begins immediately after it. Markers are optional by receiver choice, but every sender must be able to generate them when requested. Markers are included in the containing FPDU's CRC calculation when both features are enabled.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver can use a marker's pointer to locate the frame that contains it. This helps recover record boundaries when TCP segments arrive out of order or are split differently on the path.

sections.title: CRC Use and Maximum Record Size
sections.content:
An MPA implementation must implement CRC support. CRCs are enabled by default, and they can be disabled only when both endpoints indicate that preference. The RFC says CRCs should not be suppressed unless the end-to-end connection has error protection at least as strong as CRC32c, such as end-to-end IPsec integrity. A receiver must treat an FPDU with an invalid CRC as invalid.

MPA reports the Maximum ULPDU (MULPDU) that fits in an FPDU. The value depends on the effective maximum segment size, marker overhead, and padding. It must be between 128 and 64768 octets, and DDP must not submit a ULPDU larger than 64768 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: CRC checking is on by default and checks whether an FPDU was damaged. MPA also tells DDP the largest record that fits within the current transport limits.

sections.title: Startup Negotiation
sections.content:
MPA has a Startup Phase and a Full Operation Phase. During startup, the endpoints exchange an MPA Request Frame and an MPA Reply Frame without CRCs or markers. The frames identify MPA, negotiate marker and CRC use, and may carry up to 512 octets of Private Data for the upper-layer protocol.

The upper layer chooses which endpoint sends the request first and ensures that both endpoints start MPA at the same location in the TCP byte stream. A responder must validate a request before entering full operation and must receive and validate at least one FPDU before sending any. If a connection request is rejected, the responder can leave the TCP connection open for the upper layer to decide what to do.
sections.plainLanguage: The endpoints exchange request and reply frames before sending framed records. They agree on marker and CRC use, then begin full operation at the same point in the TCP stream.

sections.title: Error Semantics
sections.content:
MPA detects closed or lost TCP connections, CRC mismatches, disagreements between marker pointers and frame lengths, and invalid startup frames. After an error, it must stop passing further FPDUs on that half connection. Errors in startup frames require closing the TCP connection.

For CRC and marker errors, an optimized implementation may drop the TCP segment so TCP retransmits it. MPA does not itself close TCP for those errors; the upper layer decides whether to close the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: When framing checks fail, MPA stops passing records to DDP. For some errors, it can let TCP retransmit the affected segment.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC discusses impersonation, stream hijacking, man-in-the-middle attacks, and eavesdropping. It says end-to-end Internet Protocol Security (IPsec) is the best protection and requires an MPA-on-TCP implementation to follow the IPsec requirements in RFC 3723.

IPsec protection that ends at an intermediate tunnel does not protect against hosts between that tunnel and the peer. The RFC also warns that attacks reaching DDP and the Remote Direct Memory Access Protocol (RDMAP) buffers can result in connection loss or denial of service.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC requires the specified IPsec support to protect the connection end to end. A tunnel that ends before the peer leaves the remaining path exposed.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero when sent; ignored on receipt except for CRC calculation.

fields.name: FPDUPTR
fields.desc: Backward distance to the enclosing FPDU start, or zero between FPDUs.
